And now the part of the programme where we save you from an awkward moment abroad. Tipping. In Japan, do not do it. Leaving money on the table can be taken as an insult, and staff have been known to run after tourists to give it back. In the United States it is the opposite. Between eighteen and twenty-two per cent is normal, it is not optional in any real sense, and waiters are paid on the assumption that you will leave it. In much of Europe the service is already on the bill, and anything you add is a small round number, not a percentage. Our practical advice is simple. Ask a local, or look at the bottom of the bill before you reach for your wallet, because in a lot of countries you have already paid.

Hello, it is Ana from finance, about the trip. Two things, and then I will leave you alone. First, please keep every receipt, including the small ones. I know it is annoying, and I know a coffee is three euros, but a payment with no paper does not exist as far as we are concerned. Second, there is about a third of the budget left, which is enough if there are no surprises. One more thing, and this is the important one. Try to avoid paying in cash, because that is where the receipts disappear. Card everything, keep the paper, and send it all to me on Friday. Thank you.
